UNDER THE COUNTER

By: Nicky Troll | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From border smugglers to spaza shop counters, we go undercover to trace South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade and lift the lid on the hidden supply chain that keeps it alive.

Unique Selling Point:
** A way to tell the Story of Illegal Cigarettes with unique access
- UNDERCOVER BUYS
- EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF BORDER SMUGGLING
- Drone footage of receiving / distribution points
- Footage of past recoveries

Summary:
South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade is now so big it outperforms the legal market. Run by powerful criminal networks and fuelled by weak enforcement, it robs the state of over R24 billion a year in lost taxes. In this investigative piece, we go undercover to township spaza shops and informal markets, capturing the sale of brands priced far below the legal tax minimum – a sure giveaway of the products illicit roots.

These hidden-camera buys, are our foot in to trace the origins. But, we push deeper, posing as would-be sellers looking for a supplier. This sting aims to connect with a middle-man in the supply chain, exposing how illicit stock moves from the border into township shelves.

The next step is the origin in SA. I have exclusive border footage from Musina, showing smugglers moving contraband cigarettes from Zimbabwe into South Africa day in and day out. It’s unbelievable.

Experts and local Musina voices will unpack how outdated regulation, corruption, and porous borders keep the trade thriving, despite government promises to crack down. It’s a dangerous business, the smugglers have lookouts to secure the path along with armed watchmen ensuring the job gets done at any cost. Locals are fearful and nervous to challenge the smugglers.

This is a high-stakes story with gritty visuals: from whispered street-corner deals to brazen cross-border hauls. It’s about more than cheap smokes - it’s a multi-billion-rand criminal economy bleeding the nation dry and undermining public health. Our investigation will expose it, from the shop counter to the border fence.


Further information:
BACKGROUND
Dominates the Market
Illicit cigarettes now account for over 30% of the total market, at times even surpassing legal sales and cost the government more than ZAR 7 billion annually in lost revenue .

A porter can carry between 2-3 master cases per trip. That’s between 20000-30000 illegal cigarettes per trip.

Decades of Economic Erosion
Between 2002 and 2022, South Africa lost a staggering R119 billion in excise and VAT revenue due to illicit cigarette sales, with R110 billion lost from 2010 onward as the illegal market expanded .

Criminal Networks & Grey-Market Dynamics
ICT is propelled by organized crime, corruption, and a regulatory grey zone where legal and illegal tobacco traffic overlap. Outdated enforcement strategies fail to curb this. The trade thrives in this limbo
The smuggling routes are divided into two sectors in Musina – the East and West. The East is a free for all. At least 10 medium sized groups run porters across, with a number of smaller chancers as well – mostly at night. There is infighting amongst the groups for crossing turf. The West is run by an organised group believed to be Somali nationals at helm. This operation is run with military precision, nothing is left to chance.

KEY PLAYERS
Scouts – check out the route before porters start crossing
Look outs – in position along route during the crossings
Guards – to protect the goods – they’re armed and don’t hesitate to shoot.
Organisers – they have a number of teams crossing every day – they are in charge of logistics
Receivers – there are multiple drop off points in and around Musina
Couriers – these are the bakkies, taxis and trucks with hidden compartments that transport to other provinces – mostly tinted window taxis and low suspension bakkies running deliveries most days.

Local Impact
People in Musina know what goes, but it’s safer to look the other way. This is a high-stakes, big profit criminal network.

The smugglers cross over the Limpopo and through farming private properties. There are three groups of affected farmers:
GROUP 1 | THE VICTIMS – the smugglers have taken over the majority of the land forcing farmers to pack up and go or best case scenario to keep a small portion of the farm going while giving up the rest.
GROUP 2 | TURNING A BLIND EYE – the farm gates are left open or in some cases the smugglers have been given keys – the deal is not to damage farm land or fences in exchange for free passage. Not a deal most farmers are eager for, but they have no choice and this is the most cost effective way to away damage to property and violence.
GROUP 3 | CO-CONSPIRATORS – this is the smallest group – these farmers are part of the network – they take a cut for free passage and in some cased they even offer support in providing vehicles and transport.

Systemic Governance Gaps
Despite strong commitments, institutional weaknesses, such as low regulatory effectiveness, inclusion on the FATF Grey List, understaffed enforcement units, and inefficient border and port management hamper progress in tackling illicit trade .

SCRIPT | Under the Counter

OPENING VISUALS – NO VO.

(MACFARLANE): Musina: a border town at the edge of Limpopo. Here authority barely holds and rules are bent.


(MACFARLANE): To the East of the Beitbridge border post lies an abandoned 5,000-hectare farm with a twelve-bedroom hunting lodge. It’s owned by local businessman Hermanus Schoeman.

(HERMANUS): They sent a message to me and they said, you, you white people must now F-off from this farm because this farm belongs to us.
(MACFARLANE): Nine months ago, he packed up and left, abandoning a property worth R40-million. Returning occasionally to the shell of a once prosperous lodge is challenging. Hermanus has a reputation for standing his ground in defence of what he owns… but not on this occasion.
(HERMANUS): I gave that up. Very, very sad story.


(MACFARLANE): But what you might think is a story about a land grab… another functioning farm now neglected… is about something else entirely. Arguably far more damaging to our country.

It’s about an economy in the shadows, fuelled by a lucrative black-market trade.

And to tell the story we start in Joburg.

SMOKING INTRO VISUAL BREAK - NO VO UNDER IT

(MACFARLANE): Cigarettes are loaded with a hefty sin tax, making them an expensive habit.

An average pack of legitimate cigarettes costs R55 plus - which includes about R26 in excise tax, VAT, manufacturing costs and company profit.

But on the streets, it’s a different story.

(MACFARLANE): If you know where to look, you can get your fix at half the legal price. No tax, no control. And it's sold on almost every block.

UPSOUND
(AGENT): How much is your 20s - those golden and RG?
(SHOPKEEPER MAN1): R18.
(AGENT): R18.

UPSOUND
(TROLLIP): Hey Maccie! You well?

(MACFARLANE): Private investigator Armand Trollip tested the illicit market for us in a string of undercover purchases.

(TROLLIP): You buy the cigarettes off the shelf. No questions asked. Everything under 30 bucks. That's definitely illegal stuff. And they're not even hiding it away.

(MACFARLANE): Twelve shops across four areas in the heart of Gauteng – from the East, West and South of Johannesburg to Pretoria.

UPSOUND
(AGENT): How much, how are your prices?
(SHOPKEEPER MAN 2): R10, R12, R18, R25, R55, R60.

(MACFARLANE): It’s impossible to sell legitimate cigarettes at these prices, the tax alone should be more than what Trollip's team was charged for an entire pack.

(MACFARLANE): Were you ever able to find who the supplier is?
(TROLLIP): We weren't lucky at all – no one. They’re protecting their suppliers for sure.
(MACFARLANE): Sjoh!

(MACFARLANE): Ever the entrepreneur, this shopkeeper offered to supply an undercover buyer in bulk, when he asked about sourcing a supplier.

UPSOUND
(SHOPKEEPER LADY): We’re going to work together.

(TROLLIP): We’re probably about two-three hundred meters away to get into this one shop.
(MACFARLANE): This is the informal market of South Africa, right? Right next to a taxi.
(TROLLIP): You'll probably have a good laugh about this. The shop that we're going to is next to the police station.
(MACFARLANE): [LAUGHS]


(MACFARLANE): Hello, Salam Alaikum. Hello Ma. You’ve got cigarettes? How much is this?
(SHOPKEEPER LADY): R20.
(MACFARLANE): R20? How are you selling this for R20, Ma?
(SHOPKEEPER LADY): Passersby come in here, and they’re always looking for something cheaper now.
(MACFARLANE): Ma, this is illegal. I can't tell you to stop. It's your business, but this is not right.
(SHOPKEEPER LADY): Let me take it off the shelf.

(MACFARLANE): But shops like these, don’t provide a full picture of the scale of this criminal network. The real network masterminds stay out of reach - protecting an illicit market that not only competes, but is bigger than the legal tax paying one.

(MACFARLANE): The illegal cigarette trade robs South Africa of more than R20 billion every year. This is money meant for schools, hospitals and roads.

(MACFARLANE): Some tax-dodging brands are made in South Africa, but most are smuggled into the country. This investigation follows that supply chain.

To be clear, established manufacturers aren't responsible for this black market: this story is about the illicit flow itself - and to follow it - we’re heading north, to Musina, the main gateway from Zimbabwe into South Africa.

(MACFARLANE): We've been here before. We've told stories of illegal crossings, bribes and smuggling. But not this story. Because this illicit trade is not only dangerous but deadly.


(MACFARLANE): I’m meeting a Musina resident who moves in security circles. He knows how the networks operate, he’s seen the trade take over the town.

But talking is risky. For safety, his identity stays hidden.

(SECURITY INSIDER): In the last few months, where the cigarettes was on the outside, it started to be impacted to the community. We have adapted to live with it. And that's the saddest thing for me, to hear gunshot at night I think is a norm.
(MACFARLANE): So give me the lay of the land?
(SECURITY INSIDER): With the cigarette smuggling, especially East of Musina and the West of Musina, here two different types of operations take place. And as soon as they got the opportunity, they make use of it. They don't have a fixed pattern.

(MACFARLANE): And even a full Limpopo river doesn’t slow down the smuggling.

(SECURITY INSIDER): They don't care about the threat of the crocodiles or nothing. The aim is to get the cigarettes on SA side.
(MACFARLANE): It's like a cigarette smuggling corridor.
(SECURITY INSIDER): The western portion is known as the, the N1 for the cigarettes. It's really bad this side.

(MACFARLANE): Through a network of sources, we’ve secured never-before-seen footage.

VISUAL PAUSE

(MACFARLANE): Captured over the last three years, the footage reveals smugglers in action crossing relentlessly over privately owned land.

VISUAL PAUSE

(MACFARLANE): Night or day, it doesn’t matter. In this one minute clip, forty-nine carriers cross.

VISUAL MOMENT

(MACFARLANE): These groups cover distances of up to 20 kilometers on foot - each carrier hauling up to 30 kilograms on his back.

This informant regularly crosses paths with smugglers.

(INFORMANT SUBTITLE): Those people, they're walking as a big group.
(MACFARLANE): As a big group.
(INFORMANT SUBTITLE): Yeah. From 50 to 100 people most of the times. Those guys, mostly they have some escorts. When they walk, in front of the group there will be three guys [that are] armed. Then behind, there's another three guys again, or four guys armed to protect the group with the cigarettes. They are dangerous people because when they're at work, they don't want to be disturbed.

VISUAL BEAT

(SECURITY INSIDER): This is not just a Limpopo, Musina problem, this is a national problem. It's eating into our tax revenue.

(MACFARLANE): A thousand packs of cigarettes are carried in one run contained in two mastercases. At roughly R26 tax each, that’s a minimum of R26,000 in lost revenue for the state, every time a carrier does a drop off.

(MACFARLANE): Our sources have told us that this area is one of the hotspots. And everywhere you go, you'll find footpaths like this. And, evidence of the smugglers lives all over. And this is literally three minutes away from the town of Musina.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): To grasp the scale, I have to get off the ground and into the air.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): From above, the tracks tell the story - trails carved into privately owned land with possible entry points everywhere.

(MACFARLANE): On this border, vast stretches of land to secure, porous borders and constant pressure from smugglers leave farmers with tough choices.

(MACFARLANE): Some farmers lose everything. Others, they just turn a blind eye. And there's some that cut a deal. I'm going to meet a landowner, Hermanus Schoeman, who's had run-ins with some of these smugglers.

(MACFARLANE): Hermanus, how you?
(HERMANUS): Fine. And you?
(MACFARLANE): Lekker.
(HERMANUS): Good man.
(MACFARLANE): So is this what it's come to now?
(HERMANUS): Yeah. This is the solution to protect your fences against the smugglers.
(MACFARLANE): So is this all bulletproof?
(HERMANUS): This is all bullerproof, yeah. So, we come at night, and then we jump inside, and then at least we are protected.
(MACFARLANE): Okay, what's it like up there?
(HERMANUS): Do you want to go up there go and feel for yourself. I can even organize, we can shoot on the side here, you can get the full, the full experience.
(MACFARLANE): No, no, no. It’s fine. I'll go up. Maybe give me a gun.
Ah! Made it!
(MACFARLANE): So you've been here and you've heard dat-dat-dat-dat-dat bullets hitting this thing?
(HERMANUS): Yeah. Yeah. That's why there’s holes on the side.
(MACFARLANE): So I can see why you chose this spot - from here, you can almost see the entire farm in the valley as far as the eye can see. Right?
(HERMANUS): And at night, they are walking with small lights or with cell phone lights, so you can see them coming very far. And of course, the vehicles coming to load you can see them very far. And you can see when they stop and when they start to cut the fence and to go in.

(MACFARLANE): It's an illicit industry that's drawn in locals too.

(MACFARLANE): Who are these faceless people that you’re negotiation with, is it Zimbabweans, is it South Africans?
(HERMANUS): No, it's South Africans.
(MACFARLANE): It’s South Africans.
(HERMANUS): It's South Africans who's the bosses and getting the cigarettes into the rest of South Africa, of course in Zimbabweans sending it from that side. But the carriers are just jobless people from Zimbabwe that, that carry it.


(INFORMANT): Those people that are carrying boxes, maybe they will get R300 per trip.
(MACFARLANE): And how many trips do they do?
(INFORMANT): Maybe they do one trip a day. So, mostly they work during the week - Monday to Friday. Then, after that, they get paid on Saturday.

(SECURITY INSIDER): So if you to do that for 20 days it's R6000.
(MACFARLANE): More than the average salary that a person gets.
(SECURITY INSIDER): And it's tax free, it’s cash. And that's why the people of Musina is not standing up to it because they will be cutting their own throat.
(MACFARLANE): It's almost like politics of the stomach, right?
(SECURITY INSIDER): Correct.
(MACFARLANE): If you stop this, people don't eat because somebody here is making something.

(MACFARLANE): But survival for some, means loss for others, landowners like Hermanus pay the price. He loses game with every cut fence on his hunting farm. Five high-value animals have already escaped.

(HERMANUS): Only the buffalo bull was R100 000.
(MACFARLANE): How often was this happening?
(HERMANUS): At some stage for four months, it was basically happening every night. We were falling behind with the repairs, because they were cutting faster than what my two guys could repair the fence.

(MACFARLANE): At his wits' end, Hermanus was forced into an unprecedented step. He arranged a meeting with the people behind this smuggling network.

(HERMANUS): We came to an agreement where we said, please don't cut our fences. I gave them locks and keys for a gate on that side and a gate on this side, so that they don't need to cut my fence.

(MACFARLANE): This footage shows another courier load point, hidden deep inside private land.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): But these sites shift constantly to evade detection - getting caught means big losses. But it rarely happens.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): In the past two years, there’s been a few major recoveries in this area. In 2023, 2024 and some even this year….

But even million-rand seizures don’t slow them down - carriers march, scouts guide and guards shadow them with guns.

VISUAL PAUSE

(MACFARLANE): Do these guys even fear the police or the army?
(SECURITY INSIDER): I don't think they fear the police and the army, to be honest, because they are doing what they want to do. The last few months we realized they are carrying radios. There's a lot of drone activity here, they are flying over to check. Sometimes it’s a hundred carriers, people walking with them with AK47s. The army and the police doesn't have the fighting power to overpower these guys.

(MACFARLANE): Hermanus’ arrangement was short-lived, forcing him to man his fences with armed security guards.

(HERMANUS): They became more and more militant. They had armed escorts. It ended up where we were shooting at each other. And then I put up the bulletproof huts. We got long distance rifles with night vision so we could see at night. And then we had, a proper discussion about the situation.
(MACFARLANE): There's no middle ground.
(HERMANUS): There’s no middle ground. Now, this is what you're going to get when you come into my into my property. We tried the police, the military. So then we took it in our own hands, and we got the solution. So they are not on this farm of mine anymore, they have now moved to other, to other places.

(MACFARLANE): Ironically, they moved onto other land Hermanus owns - the Eastern property with his once thriving hunting lodge.

(HERMANUS): Normally you won’t pass the guys carrying the cigarettes here, they will be in the bush.
(MACFARLANE): So here onwards is no, no man's land here?
(HERMANUS): Still belongs to me. But not no man's land - all man's land.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): Sjoh, so this is it here?
(HERMANUS): Yeah.
(MACFARLANE): How does it feel coming back here now?
(HERMANUS): Yeah, well, it's sad, hey.
(MACFARLANE): Yeah.
(MACFARLANE): You've got no other choice but to leave, there's no way that you can fight for this?
(HERMANUS): I'm the guy that like to fight for something. But um, the problem is that you are risking your clients. I don't mind if it's me and my guys, and we have to put up a fight, then, then we do it. But you have foreigners all the time. We just couldn't risk the lives of our clients to go into the bush anymore, it would end up and then somebody has got a gun in your face.

(MACFARLANE): Since leaving the property, it’s become a hive of criminal activity with border jumpers moving through, stolen cars moving out, and contraband flowing in.

VISUAL BEAT

(MACFARLANE): And with the border fence like this? Illegal cigarettes will continue to flood the market. Case by case. Trip by trip. Because no one dares to stop it.

(HERMANUS): As long as there's so much money involved, and as long as the government don't have the real will to stop it and to do something on the on the border fence, you will never, you will never win this war.

(MACFARLANE): And as long as demand stays high and the border stays open, the trade will thrive. Under the counter. Over the border. And out of control.

Decades of Economic Erosion Between 2002 and 2022, South Africa lost a staggering R119 billion in excise and VAT revenue due to illicit cigarette sales, with R110 billion lost from 2010 onward as the illegal market expanded . Criminal Networks & Grey-Market Dynamics ICT is propelled by organized crime, corruption, and a regulatory grey zone where legal and illegal tobacco traffic overlap. Outdated enforcement strategies fail to curb this. The trade thrives in this limbo The smuggling routes are divided into two sectors in Musina – the East and West. The East is a free for all. At least 10 medium sized groups run porters across, with a number of smaller chancers as well – mostly at night. There is infighting amongst the groups for crossing turf. The West is run by an organised group believed to be Somali nationals at helm. This operation is run with military precision, nothing is left to chance. KEY PLAYERS Scouts – check out the route before porters start crossing Look outs – in position along route during the crossings Guards – to protect the goods – they’re armed and don’t hesitate to shoot. Organisers – they have a number of teams crossing every day – they are in charge of logistics Receivers – there are multiple drop off points in and around Musina Couriers – these are the bakkies, taxis and trucks with hidden compartments that transport to other provinces – mostly tinted window taxis and low suspension bakkies running deliveries most days. Local Impact People in Musina know what goes, but it’s safer to look the other way. This is a high-stakes, big profit criminal network. The smugglers cross over the Limpopo and through farming private properties. There are three groups of affected farmers: GROUP 1 | THE VICTIMS – the smugglers have taken over the majority of the land forcing farmers to pack up and go or best case scenario to keep a small portion of the farm going while giving up the rest. GROUP 2 | TURNING A BLIND EYE – the farm gates are left open or in some cases the smugglers have been given keys – the deal is not to damage farm land or fences in exchange for free passage. Not a deal most farmers are eager for, but they have no choice and this is the most cost effective way to away damage to property and violence. GROUP 3 | CO-CONSPIRATORS – this is the smallest group – these farmers are part of the network – they take a cut for free passage and in some cased they even offer support in providing vehicles and transport. Systemic Governance Gaps Despite strong commitments, institutional weaknesses, such as low regulatory effectiveness, inclusion on the FATF Grey List, understaffed enforcement units, and inefficient border and port management hamper progress in tackling illicit trade . (MACFARLANE): Musina: a border town at the edge of Limpopo. Here authority barely holds and rules are bent. (MACFARLANE): To the East of the Beitbridge border post lies an abandoned 5,000-hectare farm with a twelve-bedroom hunting lodge. It’s owned by local businessman Hermanus Schoeman. (HERMANUS): They sent a message to me and they said, you, you white people must now F-off from this farm because this farm belongs to us. (MACFARLANE): Nine months ago, he packed up and left, abandoning a property worth R40-million. Returning occasionally to the shell of a once prosperous lodge is challenging. Hermanus has a reputation for standing his ground in defence of what he owns… but not on this occasion. (HERMANUS): I gave that up. Very, very sad story. (MACFARLANE): But what you might think is a story about a land grab… another functioning farm now neglected… is about something else entirely. Arguably far more damaging to our country. It’s about an economy in the shadows, fuelled by a lucrative black-market trade. And to tell the story we start in Joburg. SMOKING INTRO VISUAL BREAK - NO VO UNDER IT (MACFARLANE): Cigarettes are loaded with a hefty sin tax, making them an expensive habit. An average pack of legitimate cigarettes costs R55 plus - which includes about R26 in excise tax, VAT, manufacturing costs and company profit. But on the streets, it’s a different story. (MACFARLANE): If you know where to look, you can get your fix at half the legal price. No tax, no control. And it's sold on almost every block. UPSOUND (AGENT): How much is your 20s - those golden and RG? (SHOPKEEPER MAN1): R18. (AGENT): R18. UPSOUND (TROLLIP): Hey Maccie! You well? (MACFARLANE): Private investigator Armand Trollip tested the illicit market for us in a string of undercover purchases. (TROLLIP): You buy the cigarettes off the shelf. No questions asked. Everything under 30 bucks. That's definitely illegal stuff. And they're not even hiding it away. (MACFARLANE): Twelve shops across four areas in the heart of Gauteng – from the East, West and South of Johannesburg to Pretoria. UPSOUND (AGENT): How much, how are your prices? (SHOPKEEPER MAN 2): R10, R12, R18, R25, R55, R60. (MACFARLANE): It’s impossible to sell legitimate cigarettes at these prices, the tax alone should be more than what Trollip's team was charged for an entire pack. (MACFARLANE): Were you ever able to find who the supplier is? (TROLLIP): We weren't lucky at all – no one. They’re protecting their suppliers for sure. (MACFARLANE): Sjoh! (MACFARLANE): Ever the entrepreneur, this shopkeeper offered to supply an undercover buyer in bulk, when he asked about sourcing a supplier. UPSOUND (SHOPKEEPER LADY): We’re going to work together. (TROLLIP): We’re probably about two-three hundred meters away to get into this one shop. (MACFARLANE): This is the informal market of South Africa, right? Right next to a taxi. (TROLLIP): You'll probably have a good laugh about this. The shop that we're going to is next to the police station. (MACFARLANE): [LAUGHS] (MACFARLANE): Hello, Salam Alaikum. Hello Ma. You’ve got cigarettes? How much is this? (SHOPKEEPER LADY): R20. (MACFARLANE): R20? How are you selling this for R20, Ma? (SHOPKEEPER LADY): Passersby come in here, and they’re always looking for something cheaper now. (MACFARLANE): Ma, this is illegal. I can't tell you to stop. It's your business, but this is not right. (SHOPKEEPER LADY): Let me take it off the shelf. (MACFARLANE): But shops like these, don’t provide a full picture of the scale of this criminal network. The real network masterminds stay out of reach - protecting an illicit market that not only competes, but is bigger than the legal tax paying one. (MACFARLANE): The illegal cigarette trade robs South Africa of more than R20 billion every year. This is money meant for schools, hospitals and roads. (MACFARLANE): Some tax-dodging brands are made in South Africa, but most are smuggled into the country. This investigation follows that supply chain. To be clear, established manufacturers aren't responsible for this black market: this story is about the illicit flow itself - and to follow it - we’re heading north, to Musina, the main gateway from Zimbabwe into South Africa. (MACFARLANE): We've been here before. We've told stories of illegal crossings, bribes and smuggling. But not this story. Because this illicit trade is not only dangerous but deadly. (MACFARLANE): I’m meeting a Musina resident who moves in security circles. He knows how the networks operate, he’s seen the trade take over the town. But talking is risky. For safety, his identity stays hidden. (SECURITY INSIDER): In the last few months, where the cigarettes was on the outside, it started to be impacted to the community. We have adapted to live with it. And that's the saddest thing for me, to hear gunshot at night I think is a norm. (MACFARLANE): So give me the lay of the land? (SECURITY INSIDER): With the cigarette smuggling, especially East of Musina and the West of Musina, here two different types of operations take place. And as soon as they got the opportunity, they make use of it. They don't have a fixed pattern. (MACFARLANE): And even a full Limpopo river doesn’t slow down the smuggling. (SECURITY INSIDER): They don't care about the threat of the crocodiles or nothing. The aim is to get the cigarettes on SA side. (MACFARLANE): It's like a cigarette smuggling corridor. (SECURITY INSIDER): The western portion is known as the, the N1 for the cigarettes. It's really bad this side. (MACFARLANE): Through a network of sources, we’ve secured never-before-seen footage. VISUAL PAUSE (MACFARLANE): Captured over the last three years, the footage reveals smugglers in action crossing relentlessly over privately owned land. VISUAL PAUSE (MACFARLANE): Night or day, it doesn’t matter. In this one minute clip, forty-nine carriers cross. VISUAL MOMENT (MACFARLANE): These groups cover distances of up to 20 kilometers on foot - each carrier hauling up to 30 kilograms on his back. This informant regularly crosses paths with smugglers. (INFORMANT SUBTITLE): Those people, they're walking as a big group. (MACFARLANE): As a big group. (INFORMANT SUBTITLE): Yeah. From 50 to 100 people most of the times. Those guys, mostly they have some escorts. When they walk, in front of the group there will be three guys [that are] armed. Then behind, there's another three guys again, or four guys armed to protect the group with the cigarettes. They are dangerous people because when they're at work, they don't want to be disturbed. VISUAL BEAT (SECURITY INSIDER): This is not just a Limpopo, Musina problem, this is a national problem. It's eating into our tax revenue. (MACFARLANE): A thousand packs of cigarettes are carried in one run contained in two mastercases. At roughly R26 tax each, that’s a minimum of R26,000 in lost revenue for the state, every time a carrier does a drop off. (MACFARLANE): Our sources have told us that this area is one of the hotspots. And everywhere you go, you'll find footpaths like this. And, evidence of the smugglers lives all over. And this is literally three minutes away from the town of Musina. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): To grasp the scale, I have to get off the ground and into the air. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): From above, the tracks tell the story - trails carved into privately owned land with possible entry points everywhere. (MACFARLANE): On this border, vast stretches of land to secure, porous borders and constant pressure from smugglers leave farmers with tough choices. (MACFARLANE): Some farmers lose everything. Others, they just turn a blind eye. And there's some that cut a deal. I'm going to meet a landowner, Hermanus Schoeman, who's had run-ins with some of these smugglers. (MACFARLANE): Hermanus, how you? (HERMANUS): Fine. And you? (MACFARLANE): Lekker. (HERMANUS): Good man. (MACFARLANE): So is this what it's come to now? (HERMANUS): Yeah. This is the solution to protect your fences against the smugglers. (MACFARLANE): So is this all bulletproof? (HERMANUS): This is all bullerproof, yeah. So, we come at night, and then we jump inside, and then at least we are protected. (MACFARLANE): Okay, what's it like up there? (HERMANUS): Do you want to go up there go and feel for yourself. I can even organize, we can shoot on the side here, you can get the full, the full experience. (MACFARLANE): No, no, no. It’s fine. I'll go up. Maybe give me a gun. Ah! Made it! (MACFARLANE): So you've been here and you've heard dat-dat-dat-dat-dat bullets hitting this thing? (HERMANUS): Yeah. Yeah. That's why there’s holes on the side. (MACFARLANE): So I can see why you chose this spot - from here, you can almost see the entire farm in the valley as far as the eye can see. Right? (HERMANUS): And at night, they are walking with small lights or with cell phone lights, so you can see them coming very far. And of course, the vehicles coming to load you can see them very far. And you can see when they stop and when they start to cut the fence and to go in. (MACFARLANE): It's an illicit industry that's drawn in locals too. (MACFARLANE): Who are these faceless people that you’re negotiation with, is it Zimbabweans, is it South Africans? (HERMANUS): No, it's South Africans. (MACFARLANE): It’s South Africans. (HERMANUS): It's South Africans who's the bosses and getting the cigarettes into the rest of South Africa, of course in Zimbabweans sending it from that side. But the carriers are just jobless people from Zimbabwe that, that carry it. (INFORMANT): Those people that are carrying boxes, maybe they will get R300 per trip. (MACFARLANE): And how many trips do they do? (INFORMANT): Maybe they do one trip a day. So, mostly they work during the week - Monday to Friday. Then, after that, they get paid on Saturday. (SECURITY INSIDER): So if you to do that for 20 days it's R6000. (MACFARLANE): More than the average salary that a person gets. (SECURITY INSIDER): And it's tax free, it’s cash. And that's why the people of Musina is not standing up to it because they will be cutting their own throat. (MACFARLANE): It's almost like politics of the stomach, right? (SECURITY INSIDER): Correct. (MACFARLANE): If you stop this, people don't eat because somebody here is making something. (MACFARLANE): But survival for some, means loss for others, landowners like Hermanus pay the price. He loses game with every cut fence on his hunting farm. Five high-value animals have already escaped. (HERMANUS): Only the buffalo bull was R100 000. (MACFARLANE): How often was this happening? (HERMANUS): At some stage for four months, it was basically happening every night. We were falling behind with the repairs, because they were cutting faster than what my two guys could repair the fence. (MACFARLANE): At his wits' end, Hermanus was forced into an unprecedented step. He arranged a meeting with the people behind this smuggling network. (HERMANUS): We came to an agreement where we said, please don't cut our fences. I gave them locks and keys for a gate on that side and a gate on this side, so that they don't need to cut my fence. (MACFARLANE): This footage shows another courier load point, hidden deep inside private land. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): But these sites shift constantly to evade detection - getting caught means big losses. But it rarely happens. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): In the past two years, there’s been a few major recoveries in this area. In 2023, 2024 and some even this year…. But even million-rand seizures don’t slow them down - carriers march, scouts guide and guards shadow them with guns. VISUAL PAUSE (MACFARLANE): Do these guys even fear the police or the army? (SECURITY INSIDER): I don't think they fear the police and the army, to be honest, because they are doing what they want to do. The last few months we realized they are carrying radios. There's a lot of drone activity here, they are flying over to check. Sometimes it’s a hundred carriers, people walking with them with AK47s. The army and the police doesn't have the fighting power to overpower these guys. (MACFARLANE): Hermanus’ arrangement was short-lived, forcing him to man his fences with armed security guards. (HERMANUS): They became more and more militant. They had armed escorts. It ended up where we were shooting at each other. And then I put up the bulletproof huts. We got long distance rifles with night vision so we could see at night. And then we had, a proper discussion about the situation. (MACFARLANE): There's no middle ground. (HERMANUS): There’s no middle ground. Now, this is what you're going to get when you come into my into my property. We tried the police, the military. So then we took it in our own hands, and we got the solution. So they are not on this farm of mine anymore, they have now moved to other, to other places. (MACFARLANE): Ironically, they moved onto other land Hermanus owns - the Eastern property with his once thriving hunting lodge. (HERMANUS): Normally you won’t pass the guys carrying the cigarettes here, they will be in the bush. (MACFARLANE): So here onwards is no, no man's land here? (HERMANUS): Still belongs to me. But not no man's land - all man's land. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): Sjoh, so this is it here? (HERMANUS): Yeah. (MACFARLANE): How does it feel coming back here now? (HERMANUS): Yeah, well, it's sad, hey. (MACFARLANE): Yeah. (MACFARLANE): You've got no other choice but to leave, there's no way that you can fight for this? (HERMANUS): I'm the guy that like to fight for something. But um, the problem is that you are risking your clients. I don't mind if it's me and my guys, and we have to put up a fight, then, then we do it. But you have foreigners all the time. We just couldn't risk the lives of our clients to go into the bush anymore, it would end up and then somebody has got a gun in your face. (MACFARLANE): Since leaving the property, it’s become a hive of criminal activity with border jumpers moving through, stolen cars moving out, and contraband flowing in. VISUAL BEAT (MACFARLANE): And with the border fence like this? Illegal cigarettes will continue to flood the market. Case by case. Trip by trip. Because no one dares to stop it. (HERMANUS): As long as there's so much money involved, and as long as the government don't have the real will to stop it and to do something on the on the border fence, you will never, you will never win this war. (MACFARLANE): And as long as demand stays high and the border stays open, the trade will thrive. Under the counter. Over the border. And out of control. ENDS

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From border smugglers to spaza shop counters, we go undercover to trace South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade and lift the lid on the hidden supply chain that keeps it alive.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: ** A way to tell the Story of Illegal Cigarettes with unique access - UNDERCOVER BUYS - EXCLUSIVE FOOTAGE OF BORDER SMUGGLING - Drone footage of receiving / distribution points - Footage of past recoveries
metadata.Summary: South Africa’s illicit cigarette trade is now so big it outperforms the legal market. Run by powerful criminal networks and fuelled by weak enforcement, it robs the state of over R24 billion a year in lost taxes. In this investigative piece, we go undercover to township spaza shops and informal markets, capturing the sale of brands priced far below the legal tax minimum – a sure giveaway of the products illicit roots. These hidden-camera buys, are our foot in to trace the origins. But, we push deeper, posing as would-be sellers looking for a supplier. This sting aims to connect with a middle-man in the supply chain, exposing how illicit stock moves from the border into township shelves. The next step is the origin in SA. I have exclusive border footage from Musina, showing smugglers moving contraband cigarettes from Zimbabwe into South Africa day in and day out. It’s unbelievable. Experts and local Musina voices will unpack how outdated regulation, corruption, and porous borders keep the trade thriving, despite government promises to crack down. It’s a dangerous business, the smugglers have lookouts to secure the path along with armed watchmen ensuring the job gets done at any cost. Locals are fearful and nervous to challenge the smugglers. This is a high-stakes story with gritty visuals: from whispered street-corner deals to brazen cross-border hauls. It’s about more than cheap smokes - it’s a multi-billion-rand criminal economy bleeding the nation dry and undermining public health. Our investigation will expose it, from the shop counter to the border fence.
